archetypes.name: Distrustful but content insiders
archetypes.text: These respondents combine low interpersonal and institutional trust with a comfortable personal life. They feel little trust in people or institutions and are dissatisfied with how democracy works, yet they rate their finances as stable or improving and report being pretty happy. Many describe the economy as bad while still seeing their own situation as fine, and they are uneasy about AI and robots while often treating technology in mixed or contradictory ways. Routine socializing with friends or relatives runs alongside a wary, skeptical view of the wider world, which is the surprising pairing that defines the group.

archetypes.name: Distrustful financially strained skeptics
archetypes.text: People who distrust nearly every institution and other people, feel their finances are stuck, and see the economy as bad, yet still report being pretty happy. They tend to view life as routine while keeping close family ties, often seeing family time as more reliable than friendships. They consistently reject the idea that men's work harms family life or hold mixed views on it, express unease about AI and robots, and frequently call federal taxes too high. Their combination of deep institutional mistrust with personal contentment is the surprising core of this pattern.

archetypes.name: Distrustful but engaged skeptics
archetypes.text: People who are deeply dissatisfied with American democracy and the economy, yet remain politically engaged and actively verify political information online. Their financial outlook is bleak and family income feels far below average, but their general personal contentment is not uniformly low. A notable pairing is strong enthusiasm for automation and AI alongside a wish for more science spending and a fondness for routine, low-key social life. They tend to trust in institutions selectively, rather than uniformly high or low, and their views of taxes and social class are often inconsistent with their economic distress.
